The Qing state was the poorest, most isolated, and least advanced. Chu Xiao was more powerful, but none of these states eventually united China. Instead, the isolated and marginalized Qing state came to conquer. The question is why this happened.

Elites within these states competed against each other through warfare to maintain a status quo. This led to the idea of Chinese chess, which regulated warfare in a ritualized manner. When they went to war, they had to respect each other's rules despite the fact that war should be about killing the enemy, not following rules.

Another piece of evidence is The Art of War, written during this time. It is one of the stupidest books ever because it focuses on cheating in a heavily regulated game—using spies and maintaining high guard. In actual war, none of these things work.

To win a war, you must be completely committed to victory (total warfare), ensure talented officers rise to power through meritocracy, and make sure your soldiers are happy. If the status quo favors maintaining family power, innovative generals will be eliminated as threats. The third principle is to destroy enemy civil centers by sieging their cities, targeting food supplies and soldiers, killing civilians, overstretching the enemy's supply lines, dividing them, striking fear in them, and killing their gods.

This pattern of warfare was used by many conquerors like the Romans, Persians, Aztecs, Mongols, and others. When these states weren't at war with each other, they were intermarried friends maintaining a status quo through ritualized warfare. Mesopotamia, as the cradle of civilization, saw the first city-states emerge, developing colonies that eventually came into conflict but remained friendly, intermarrying elites creating highly ritualized warfare where attacking temples was forbidden because gods lived there, yet all their wealth was in them.
